name: Dajia Zhenlan Temple
address: No. 158, Shuntian Rd, Dajia District, Taichung City
description: Every third lunar month, a Mazu palanquin sets out on foot with hundreds of thousands of followers — nine days and eight nights, more than 300 kilometers across the four counties and cities of Taichung, Changhua, Yunlin, and Chiayi. This is Dajia Zhenlan Temple's 'Dajia Mazu Pilgrimage,' ranked by the Discovery Channel as one of the world's three great religious events. Standing in Dajia District, Taichung City, Zhenlan Temple is dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother) and is the best-known Mazu temple in Taiwan, a stronghold of Mazu faith. In the basement beneath its gleaming golden halls sits a solid-gold 'Golden Mazu' weighing 276 kilograms, the temple's greatest treasure. To feel the almost fevered devotion the Taiwanese hold for Mazu, this is where it begins.
history: The story starts with a deity statue that crossed the sea. By tradition, in 1730 during the Yongzheng reign, the Fujian Meizhou immigrant Lin Yongxing reverently brought a Mazu statue to Taiwan and settled in Dajia — the beginning of Zhenlan Temple. Over the following two centuries the temple was expanded and rebuilt many times, and the major reconstruction of 1980 set the grand scale of its halls today. What truly made Dajia Mazu famous throughout Taiwan is the pilgrimage that has never once lapsed year after year — wherever the palanquin passes, the streets empty of everything but people, as worshippers crawl beneath it and reach out to steady it, seeking just a touch of Mazu's protection. Today this pilgrimage is far more than a religious event; it gathers the emotion of all Taiwanese society and has become the most vivid emblem of Taiwanese folk faith.

name: Beigang Chaotian Temple
address: No. 178, Zhongshan Rd, Beigang Township, Yunlin County
description: Say the words 'Beigang Mazu,' and more than a thousand Mazu temples across Taiwan prick up their ears — Beigang Chaotian Temple in Beigang Township, Yunlin County, is a stronghold of Mazu faith in Taiwan and the pilgrimage 'ancestral temple' for countless Mazu temples, a status so lofty it is listed as a National Monument. Dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother), Chaotian Temple has divided-incense branches around the globe, and every third lunar month at Mazu's birthday, pilgrimage groups from everywhere flood this little town — gongs and drums thundering, incense curling — carrying the 'Mazu frenzy' to its height. The temple's stone carving and cut-porcelain work preserve splendid Qing-dynasty architectural art; the Zhongshan Road out front is the famous street of wedding cakes and sesame oil, a stretch of traditional good flavors.
history: In 1694, during the Kangxi reign, the Chan master Shubi crossed the sea from the Chaotian Pavilion in Meizhou carrying a gilded statue of Mazu and built a temple to enshrine her in Beigang — the beginning of one of Taiwan's oldest Mazu temples. By the Qing dynasty, Chaotian Temple held the exalted status of 'head temple of Mazu faith in Taiwan,' receiving imperial titles and bestowed plaques from successive Qing courts. Over the centuries the temple was renovated and expanded again and again, its cut-porcelain and Koji pottery decoration exquisite beyond compare, at last becoming a National Monument. From the 15th of the first lunar month through the third month, Mazu temples from across Taiwan come to 'cut incense' here, the town wreathed in smoke and ringing with gongs and drums; and the 'palanquin blasting' rite, in which worshippers set off vast volleys of firecrackers beneath the divine palanquin, is one of the most intense and spectacular temple scenes in all Taiwan.

name: Lugang Tianhou Temple
address: No. 430, Zhongshan Rd, Lukang Township, Changhua County
description: There is only one in all Taiwan — Lugang Tianhou Temple enshrines the founding Holy Mother statue from the ancestral temple in Meizhou, the thing this temple in Lukang Township, Changhua County, is proudest of. Dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother), its statue has been darkened to a glossy black by centuries of incense smoke, affectionately called 'Black-Faced Mazu.' The temple is grand in scale, its wood and stone carving all from master hands, and the 'Eight-Trigram Caisson Ceiling' of the main hall is a jewel of Taiwanese craftsmanship. To step inside is to step into the prosperous old dream of 'first Tainan, second Lukang, third Manka.' Each new year, worshippers vie to light 'Bright Lamps' and 'settle the year' (an taisui), so that a spot is often hard to find.
history: In 1725, during the Yongzheng reign, the local gentry of Lukang and Quanzhou merchants jointly funded the building of this Tianhou Temple, dedicated to the Heavenly Holy Mother. Lukang was then the largest trading port in central Taiwan — 'first Tainan, second Lukang, third Manka' says it all — and the Tianhou Temple stood at the heart of the old street, watching over two centuries of commercial rise and fall. It was renovated and expanded many times through the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns, then thoroughly rebuilt in the Taisho era under Japanese rule, setting its present layout. The Qing-dynasty plaque 'De Jing Jing Bo' and several stone stelae it preserves are precious relics. Today the Tianhou Temple joins with Lukang Old Street, the 'Breast-Touching Lane,' and the 'Nine-Turns Lane' to form a complete historic district — the finest window onto Qing-era Taiwanese trading-port culture.

name: Baishatun Gongtian Temple
address: No. 8, Baidong Li, Tongxiao Township, Miaoli County
description: No one knows which way Mazu will go today — and that is exactly what makes Baishatun Gongtian Temple so captivating. In Tongxiao Township, Miaoli County, Gongtian Temple is dedicated to the 'soft-bodied' Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother) and is one of the most strong-willed Mazu temples in Taiwan. Its annual walking pilgrimage to Beigang Chaotian Temple follows no fixed route at all; the direction is decided entirely by Mazu's palanquin — nicknamed the 'Pink Supercar' — improvising as it goes, full of mystery and surprise. The pilgrimage procession moves fast and urgently, and often turns into schools, hospitals, or private homes to give blessings, scattering Mazu's approachable compassion into ordinary households all along the way.
history: During the Daoguang reign (around the 1830s), the fishermen of Baishatun pooled their funds to build a simple straw hut to Mazu along Miaoli's coast. The people here have made their living from the sea for generations, and Mazu faith was their most important spiritual support in facing wind and wave. The straw hut was rebuilt many times before reaching the scale of today's Gongtian Temple. What truly sets Baishatun Mazu apart is the 'pilgrimage' tradition that has never once lapsed — each first lunar month, Mazu's palanquin walks from Baishatun to Beigang Chaotian Temple in Yunlin and back, a round trip of some 400 kilometers over eight or nine days. Unlike Dajia Mazu, Baishatun Mazu decides her own route entirely, signaling the way through the swaying of her palanquin, walking a different path every year — which is why she is hailed as 'the Mazu with the strongest character.' In recent years the followers walking behind this palanquin have surpassed 100,000.

name: Changhua Nanyao Temple
description: A Mazu temple hiding Greek column capitals, Japanese black tiles, and a Western dormer window — this is the most astonishing sight at Changhua Nanyao Temple in Changhua City. Dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother) and affectionately known as 'Changhua Ma,' Nanyao Temple's main hall is traditional Minnan architecture, yet its rear 'Guanyin Hall' is deeply influenced by Western architecture — a fusion of East and West extremely rare among Taiwan's temples, of exceptional artistic value. Nanyao Temple also has the largest Mazu association organization in Taiwan, and its annual 'Bengang Pilgrimage,' long in history, preserves ancient rites such as the 'Changing of the Dragon Robe,' a living fossil of Taiwan's pilgrimage culture.
history: The story opens with an incense pouch. During the Qianlong reign, a potter named Yang Qian carried a Mazu incense pouch for others to worship, and as the miracles grew renowned, more and more followers gathered, until at last Nanyao Temple was built in 1738, the third year of Qianlong. It was one of the earliest Mazu temples to make the pilgrimage to Bengang, pioneering the cross-county pilgrimage culture. In the years that followed, Nanyao Temple's lay organization, the 'Mazu Association,' grew ever larger, its influence spreading across central Taiwan. From a single small incense pouch to the largest Mazu association in Taiwan, Nanyao Temple has witnessed how Taiwan's pilgrimage culture grew from folk faith into a force that binds a community together.

name: Taichung Lecheng Temple
address: No. 48, Hanxi St, East District, Taichung City
description: The longest Mazu pilgrimage in all Taiwan is right here — the Hanxi Mazu 'Procession of the Eighteen Villages' runs for a full 22 days. Commonly called the 'Hanxi Mazu Temple,' Taichung Lecheng Temple in Taichung's East District is the oldest Mazu temple in central Taichung, listed as a national third-grade historic site and dedicated to Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother). Rebuilt under the master craftsman Chen Yingbin, its wood and stone carving are exquisite. Beyond Mazu's efficacy, Lecheng Temple's 'Yue Lao Hall' is famous across Taiwan, hailed as 'the most effective Matchmaker in central Taiwan,' drawing countless single men and women each year to pray for love and joining together many a couple. To pray to Mazu and seek a good match too — here, both wishes are answered at once.
history: During the Jiaqing reign (around the 1810s), worshippers from the Lukang area of Changhua pooled their funds to build a small temple beside the Han Stream — the forerunner of Lecheng Temple. As the area was reclaimed and developed, the temple was gradually expanded and more deities enshrined, until it became the most important center of faith along the Han Stream. Under Japanese rule the temple engaged the master craftsman Chen Yingbin to lead a large-scale reconstruction, his consummate wood and stone carving setting the architectural layout of today; after the war it was renovated again and a rear hall added. The temple still preserves Qing-dynasty stelae, plaques, and other relics recording the footsteps of the early settlers. From a small temple by the Han Stream to a center of faith whose incense endures and whose procession winds through eighteen villages, Lecheng Temple has always been bound tightly to the daily faith and community life of local people.

name: Zhushan Zinan Temple
address: No. 40, Dagong St., Zhushan Township, Nantou County
description: 'Borrowing' 600 NT dollars from the Earth God is the most famous thing about Zhushan Zinan Temple. In Zhushan Township, Nantou County, Zinan Temple is the most famous 'God of Wealth temple' in Taiwan, dedicated to the Earth God (Tudigong) and the God of Wealth. Worshippers borrow 600 dollars from the Earth God as 'Money Mother' to tuck into their wallets so that money will multiply endlessly, and if fortune truly comes the next year, they repay double. Every Lunar New Year the queues to borrow this 'fortune money' stretch for kilometers, becoming the largest tourist event in Nantou County. The temple also used its incense-offering funds to build a golden bamboo-shoot-shaped 'Golden Rooster Restroom,' crowned the most luxurious public toilet in Taiwan and, unexpectedly, a sight in its own right.
history: In 1745, during the Qianlong reign, the residents around Zhushan built a small shrine to worship the Earth God who watched over the community — the beginning of Zinan Temple. What truly made this little temple famous throughout Taiwan is the tradition of 'borrowing fortune money' — the Money Mother borrowed from the Earth God was said to be uncommonly effective, and word spread from one to ten and ten to a hundred, until worshippers came from all over Taiwan and the incense burned brighter year by year. The temple made wise use of its followers' donations, continually improving the surrounding environment and facilities — even building a public toilet gleaming with gold. And so a small shrine to the Earth God became the most important tourist and religious center in Zhushan, Nantou.

name: Songboling Shoutian Temple
address: No. 118, Songshan St, Mingjian Township, Nantou County
description: Stand atop Songboling at the southern end of the Bagua Mountain range, and the Jianan Plain unfolds at your feet — this is the 'Songling Vista' unique to Songboling Shoutian Temple. In Mingjian Township, Nantou County, Shoutian Temple is one of the head ancestral temples (zumiao) of Xuantian Shangdi faith in Taiwan, dedicated to Xuantian Shangdi, with divided-incense branches numbering in the thousands and incense burning fervently. Around the birthday of Xuantian Shangdi on the 3rd day of the 3rd lunar month, pilgrimage groups from across Taiwan arrive in an endless stream, the performance troupes lively and dazzling — one of the great events of Taiwan's religious world. To climb high and gaze afar, and to pay respects at an ancestral temple as well — this place is worth a special trip.
history: Shoutian Temple sits high atop Songboling at the southern end of the Bagua Mountain range, dedicated to Xuantian Shangdi, a center of faith established by early settlers as they opened up this land in the Qing dynasty. On the strength of its reputation for efficacy, it gradually grew into one of the most important ancestral temples of Xuantian Shangdi faith in Taiwan; over the centuries its divided incense has spread across the whole island to as many as several thousand branches — Xuantian Shangdi temples everywhere organize groups each year to return to Songboling to pay homage at the ancestral temple, forming an unbroken network of pilgrimage. Each year at the birthday of Xuantian Shangdi on the 3rd of the 3rd lunar month, the mountain rings with gongs and drums and gathers performance troupes from across Taiwan, dressing this ancestral temple as the liveliest religious celebration in central Taiwan. The sweeping view of the Songling Vista, together with incense passed down generation after generation, has made Shoutian Temple a holy site in the hearts of Xuantian Shangdi's followers.

name: Beigang Wude Palace
address: No. 330, Huasheng Rd, Beigang Township, Yunlin County
description: To pray for wealth, business people come here — Beigang Wude Palace is the founding ancestral temple of the Five Road Wealth God faith in Taiwan, the largest of its kind, in Beigang Township, Yunlin County. Dedicated to the Heavenly Official Martial God of Wealth Zhao Gongming, Wude Palace is majestic in scale, and it holds a 'Sky Treasury' gold furnace several stories high, said to be the largest in the world, dedicated to burning 'Treasury-Replenishing' paper money. This is a must-visit sanctuary for business owners and entrepreneurs, its incense burning fervently, and the 'Money Mother' coins it distributes each New Year draw tens of thousands to queue. Pray for wealth, replenish your treasury, and receive Money Mother — all in one stop.
history: Beigang Wude Palace is dedicated to the Heavenly Official Martial God of Wealth Zhao Gongming — the 'Central Road' Wealth God who commands the Five Road Wealth Gods of the east, west, south, north, and center. Beigang has been the most important commercial town in the Yunlin-Chiayi region since the Qing dynasty, and business people revered the Martial God of Wealth with special devotion, so that Wude Palace's incense burned ever brighter with this fervent wish for prosperity. After many expansions and renovations, and especially after a large-scale reconstruction in the Republican era, Wude Palace became widely known as the 'founding ancestral temple of the Five Road Wealth God' and one of the most famous God of Wealth temples in Taiwan. In its main hall Zhao Gongming is enshrined as the Central Road Martial God of Wealth, flanked by the four Wealth Gods of the east, west, south, and north. Each year at the Martial God of Wealth's birthday on the 15th of the 3rd lunar month, worshippers from across Taiwan pour in, and the temple's tradition of distributing 'fortune money' draws great crowds of wealth-seekers. Beigang Wude Palace was also among the first temples in Taiwan to introduce 'online lamp-lighting' and 'app fortune-drawing,' bringing this ancient Wealth God faith into the digital age.

name: Taichung Fahua Temple
address: No. 180, Fahua St., South Dist., Taichung City
description: A candidate's amulet of wisdom is here at Taichung Fahua Temple. In Taichung's South District and dedicated to Manjushri Bodhisattva, Fahua Temple is a long-established Buddhist temple in the Taichung area. Manjushri symbolizes wisdom, riding a blue lion and wielding a sword to cut through ignorance and open the mind — and every exam season, students come here to pray for a clear head and success on the roll. The grounds are quiet and secluded, the architecture blending traditional and modern styles, and the temple regularly holds Buddhist lectures and meditation activities — a place in the bustling city where one can settle the mind.
history: Fahua Temple began as a small Guanyin temple in the Zhugaocuo settlement during the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty. Under Japanese rule it was rebuilt as a Japanese-style Buddhist temple, named 'Fahua Temple,' and placed under the Myoshinji branch of the Japanese Rinzai school, for a time wholly Japanese in character. After World War II, Taiwanese monks took it over and gradually drew it back into the tradition of Chinese Buddhism. In the 1970s the temple carried out a large-scale reconstruction, achieving the grand appearance of today. Its main hall now enshrines Shakyamuni Buddha, with Guanyin Bodhisattva and Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva alongside, and the temple actively promotes Buddhist education and social charity, regularly holding Dharma assemblies and meditation courses — one of the most historically rich Buddhist temples in central Taichung.

name: Shanbian Mazu Temple
address: No. 108-3, Shanbian, Houlong Township, Miaoli County
description: One Mazu, for decades with no temple of her own — this is the most moving devotion of Shanbian Mazu in Houlong Township, Miaoli County. Shanbian Mazu (the Heavenly Holy Mother) long kept the singular tradition of 'a deity without a temple,' hosted in turn in the home of the serving incense keeper (luzhu), until a temporary temple was finally built for her enthronement in 2013; a permanent temple is now being planned. Shanbian Mazu shares a sisterly bond with Baishatun Mazu, and for more than a century the two have insisted on sharing a single palanquin on the pilgrimage to Beigang — an indispensable presence in the procession. Her palanquin is light and nimble, often making startling moves that draw gasps from the crowd.
history: Shanbian Mazu's exact origins can no longer be traced, for the early years left no written record, but by rough estimate she has been in Taiwan for at least 300 years. For generations Shanbian Mazu followed a 'yearly rotating incense keeper' system — each year a keeper was chosen by casting divination blocks, and that keeper reverently hosted the deity in his own home. This form of faith, 'a deity without a temple,' is utterly different from the ordinary great temple. Since 1953, Shanbian Mazu has each year shared a single palanquin with the Mazu of Baishatun Gongtian Temple, walking on foot to Beigang Chaotian Temple on pilgrimage — an unbroken tradition of more than 70 years. Only in 2013, when Shanbian Mazu was enthroned in a temporary temple, did the decades-long tradition of rotating worship come to an end; now the community is working together to build a permanent temple, so that this Mazu, adrift for centuries, may at last have a home.

name: Xiangtianhu Pasta'ay Ceremonial Ground
address: Xiangtianhu, Donghe Village, Nanzhuang Township, Miaoli County
description: The lake surface flickers in and out of the morning mist, and along its shore a mournful, ancient ritual song echoes through the night — this is Xiangtianhu (Lake Facing Heaven), set in a mountain basin about 738 meters above sea level, the primary ceremonial ground of the Saisiyat people's Pasta'ay (Ritual of the Short Spirits), and the most mysterious and moving sacred site of indigenous ceremony in Taiwan. Ringed by mountains, the scenery is dreamlike and unreal. The Pasta'ay is held as a minor ritual every two years and a grand one every ten, running for three continuous days and nights by the lakeside, using solemn ritual songs and slow steps to repent to, give thanks to, and pray to the spirits of the ancient ta'ay people. The ritual is listed as an Important Folk Cultural Asset of Taiwan; beside the ceremonial ground, the Saisiyat Pasta'ay Museum displays vital ritual objects such as hip bells and ceremonial flags.
history: The origins of the Pasta'ay reach back hundreds, even thousands of years. Legend tells that in ancient times a people of tiny stature but immense strength, the ta'ay, lived side by side with the Saisiyat and taught them the arts of farming and of song and dance. But the ta'ay came to harass the Saisiyat's women again and again, until the tribe, pushed past endurance, tampered with the mountain-loquat-tree bridge leading to the ta'ay's dwelling, and the ta'ay fell and drowned as they crossed. Before dying, the ta'ay left a curse, and from then on the Saisiyat suffered failed harvests and unending calamity. To quiet the resentment of the dead and pray for good harvests, the Saisiyat began holding the Pasta'ay at Xiangtianhu. The songs of the ritual are said to be the very ones the ta'ay taught on the verge of death, their melodies mournful and ancient — a precious living fossil of oral literature. To this day, the Xiangtianhu ceremonial ground still keeps this ancient ritual tradition, the most important sacred site for the passing-on of Saisiyat culture.

name: Zhunan Wugu Temple
address: No. 16, Wugu St, Zhunan Township, Miaoli County
description: Ride the train through Zhunan, look out the window, and a 156-Taiwanese-foot statue of Shennong appears out of nowhere. That is Wugu Temple. Finished in 1993 and standing behind the main hall, the giant figure has become the most recognizable landmark in Zhunan — you do not need the timetable; when you see him, you have arrived. Formally the Zhunan-Toufen-Zaoqiao Wugu Temple, it enshrines Shennong, the Divine Farmer, and is worshipped jointly by the Hoklo and Hakka communities of Zhunan, Sanwan, Toufen, and Zaoqiao — a shared arrangement that was rare in an era of sharp ethnic lines. Shennong governs farming and medicine, and for two centuries every harvest here has been reported to him first.
history: In 1739, Lin Er-shun of Quanzhou led some thirty settlers of both Fujianese and Cantonese origin to sign an agreement with local indigenous people and open land along the Zhonggang River; that same year they began worshipping Shennong — cultivation first, faith alongside it. In 1797 landholders including Zhang Zheng-yang, Zhang San, and Wang Xian proposed a temple, and Wugu Temple had a permanent hall at last. An incense division went to the Sanwan Wugu Temple in 1851, and in 1874 the building was rebuilt with a donors' stele that still records who paid and who labored. In 1993 the giant Shennong behind the main hall was completed, turning a two-century-old farming faith into the most conspicuous marker beside the railway.

name: Lugu Fenghuangshan Temple
address: No. 12-1, Miaokou Ln, Lugu Township, Nantou County
description: The deity here carries the word "shame" in his name — there may be no other god in Taiwan named for his own regret. Cankui Zushi, born Pan Liao-quan, attained the Way on Mount Yinna in Guangdong; before he died he felt he had failed to deliver all beings from suffering, and told his disciples to carve the word "ashamed" on his pagoda. Fenghuangshan Temple, founded in the Jiaqing era, is the heart of his worship in the mountains of Nantou. For the Han settlers who first pushed inland he was the most practical of gods — miasma, wild animals, losing the trail: all of it was his to handle. The temple sits in a lane in Fenghuang village, cool with elevation, quiet enough to hear wind moving through the tea fields.
history: Fenghuangshan Temple was founded in the Jiaqing era, exactly when Han settlers were pushing into the mountains of Nantou. Work parties carried the incense of Cankui Zushi with them, because the three things they feared most going inland — miasma, wild animals, losing the way — were said to be his to govern. Reaching this place and finding the soil rich and the landscape like home, they built thatched shelters, stayed, and enshrined the incense they had carried; that was the temple in its earliest form. Two centuries on, Lugu has turned from frontier to tea country, and the temple remains the center of his worship in these mountains. On the sixth day of the first lunar month, his feast day, Hakka families return from across Taiwan and the mountain road fills with people.
